In this video, you'll learn what the Claude API is, how it works, and how to build your first Claude-powered application — step by step, from your API key to production.
So, what exactly is the Claude API?
The Claude API lets developers build Claude directly into their own products — websites, mobile apps, internal tools, and automated workflows.
Instead of chatting in the Claude app, your code sends a request, and Claude sends back a response.
You pay only for what you use, measured in tokens — and you get access to the same powerful Claude models.
Companies use it for customer support, document analysis, coding assistants, content creation, and much more.
Let's see how a request travels through the API.
First, your application prepares a message — for example, a question from one of your users.
Your code sends it to Anthropic, as an HTTPS request to the Messages endpoint.
Claude reads the request, and generates a response.
The API returns the result as structured JSON, including the text and the number of tokens used.
And finally, your application shows the answer to your user. The whole round trip often takes just seconds.
Step zero is choosing the right model. Claude comes in several model families.
Claude Opus is the most capable choice for complex reasoning, coding, and agents — and it's the recommended default.
Claude Sonnet balances strong intelligence with speed, for everyday production work.
And Claude Haiku is the fastest and lowest-cost option, perfect for high-volume, simple tasks.
This chart shows list prices per million tokens at the time of this video. Output tokens cost more than input tokens, so always check the current pricing page before you plan your budget.
To understand costs and limits, you need to understand tokens.
A token is a small piece of text — often part of a word. Claude reads and writes text as tokens.
Input tokens are everything you send: your instructions, the conversation, and any documents.
Output tokens are everything Claude writes back in its answer.
And the context window is the total amount Claude can consider at once — up to one million tokens on current models. That's enough for very long documents.
Now let's build. Step one: get your API key.
First, sign in to the Claude Console, at console dot anthropic dot com.
Next, create an API key. This key identifies your account, so treat it like a password.
Store it safely, in an environment variable — never directly in your code, and never in a public repository.
And set up spending limits and billing alerts in the Console, so there are no surprises.
Step two: install an official SDK, a software development kit.
Anthropic provides official SDKs for Python, TypeScript and JavaScript, and Java.
There are also SDKs for Go, Ruby, C sharp, and PHP.
And if you prefer, you can call the API directly over HTTP, using a tool like curl. In this video, we'll use Python.
Step three: send your first request. It only takes a few lines of code.
First, create a client. It automatically reads your API key from the environment.
Then choose the model, and set max tokens — the maximum length of the answer.
Add a system prompt to set Claude's role, and a list of messages — here, a single question from the user.
Finally, read the response, and print the text blocks. Congratulations — you've just built your first Claude app!
Step four: understand the response.
Every response has an ID, and tells you which model answered.
The content is a list of blocks. Text blocks hold Claude's answer.
The stop reason tells you why Claude stopped — for example, end turn when it finished naturally, or max tokens if it ran out of room.
And the usage section reports the input and output tokens — exactly what you'll be billed for.
Step five: build conversations, with system prompts and message history.
Level one is the system prompt. It sets Claude's role, rules, and context for the whole conversation.
Level two is the message history. The API doesn't remember previous requests, so for a conversation, you send the full list of user and assistant messages every time.
Level three is the request settings, like max tokens and the effort level, which controls how deeply Claude thinks.
Together, these give you full control over how Claude behaves.
Step six: stream the response, for a faster experience.
Instead of waiting for the full answer, streaming sends the text piece by piece, as Claude writes it.
In Python, you open a stream with messages dot stream.
Then you loop over the text stream, and display each piece immediately.
Streaming is recommended for long answers. Your users see progress right away, and it avoids timeouts on long requests.
Step seven: give Claude tools. Tool use lets Claude call your own functions, to get data or take actions.
First, Claude decides it needs a tool, and returns a tool use request, with the tool's name and inputs.
Then your code runs the actual function — for example, looking up the weather, or querying a database.
Next, you send the result back to Claude, as a tool result.
And Claude uses that result to continue — calling more tools, or writing the final answer. This loop is the foundation of every AI agent.
Here's what that looks like in code.
First, describe each tool with a name, a clear description, and an input schema.
Then call the API in a loop, passing your tools along with the messages.
When the stop reason is tool use, run the requested tools.
And send back the results as tool result blocks. When Claude stops asking for tools, you have your final answer.
Step eight: explore the power features of the API.
Vision lets Claude read images and PDF documents — like charts, invoices, or scanned forms.
Structured outputs make Claude return JSON that matches your exact schema, so your code can rely on it.
Prompt caching reuses long, repeated content, like a big system prompt, to cut costs and speed up responses.
The Batches API processes large volumes of requests asynchronously, at half the regular price.
Citations let Claude point to the exact sentences in your documents that support its answer.
And server tools, like web search and code execution, run directly on Anthropic's infrastructure.
Step nine: get ready for production.
Handle errors gracefully. The official SDKs automatically retry temporary errors, like rate limits and server errors.
Respect rate limits, which depend on your usage tier, and grow as your usage grows.
Control costs, by choosing the right model, caching repeated prompts, and using batches for work that isn't urgent.
And monitor everything in the Console — your usage, your costs, and your logs.
Here are six best practices for building with the Claude API.
One: keep your API keys secret, and rotate them regularly.
Two: start with the most capable model, then optimize for speed and cost once it works.
Three: use streaming for long responses.
Four: cache stable content, like long system prompts and documents.
Five: always validate tool inputs and model outputs before you act on them.
And six: build a test set, and measure quality every time you change a prompt or a model.
Let's recap in one line: request, response, build.
With a few lines of code, the Claude API lets you bring Claude's intelligence into your own products — safely, reliably, and at scale.
